query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled in situ substrate preheating during the laser additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce cooling rate and thermal gradients, thereby suppressing compositional segregation and residual stress development while lowering defect formation, which in turn improves the alloy’s overall mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock that, when processed conventionally, exhibits rapid solidification-induced segregation, high residual stresses, and defect formation (e.g., cracks, pores).
generation.intervention: Implement a substrate preheating step (targeting an optimized temperature in the range of roughly 200–300 °C) during the additive manufacturing process (such as L-PBF or DED).
generation.conditions: This intervention is intended for additive manufacturing setups where laser power, scan speed, and layer thickness typical for AlCrFeNiSi processing are maintained; it assumes the temperature can be controlled without inducing detrimental grain growth or unwanted phase evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform and refined melt pool solidification that promotes homogeneous grain structures and minimizes the formation of localized compositional inhomogeneities and high-density dislocation areas at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Preheating reduces the thermal gradient between the molten metal and the substrate, slowing down the cooling rate. This controlled cooling minimizes rapid compositional changes and thermal contraction, decreasing both residual stress acquisition and the formation of defects, while facilitating improved diffusion to homogenize the elemental distribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to parts made under conventional (room temperature) conditions, specimens manufactured with substrate preheating will exhibit lower residual stress levels, reduced elemental segregation and defect density, and improved mechanical properties such as higher yield strength and better ductility.
generation.baseline: Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi parts produced by laser additive manufacturing without substrate preheating, which typically show rapid solidification effects, significant segregation, residual thermal stresses, and a higher incidence of defects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for additive manufacturing processes (e.g., L-PBF, DED) using cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi under processing conditions where moderate preheating does not inadvertently cause grain coarsening or unwanted phase changes. Its applicability may decrease if preheating temperatures are so high that they alter the intended microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on observations from studies on heat treatment relieﬁcation in eutectic high-entropy alloys (PMC12113129::web::000::abstract) and the beneficial effects of in situ thermal management in reducing residual stresses in additively manufactured tool steels (PMC12654052::web::005::1_introduction). New here is the application of substrate preheating to cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi, where the precise optimal temperature range and quantitative improvements remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using identical laser additive manufacturing parameters except for substrate temperature: one set fabricated under standard room-temperature conditions and the other with substrate preheating (targeting ~200–300 °C). Post-fabrication, perform comparative analyses on the microstructure (using SEM/EBSD and EDS), assess residual stresses (via X-ray diffraction or equivalent techniques), and evaluate mechanical properties through tensile testing.
measurements: Residual stress levels (e.g., XRD-based stress analysis)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in reduced residual stress, decreased segregation and defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. Additively manufactured H13 typically solidifies into a martensitic matrix with retained austenite and carbides, but the steep thermal gradients and cyclic reheating between layers cause high residual stresses, porosity, and cracking; hence, the routine relies on post-build stress relief and tempering. While substrate preheating and in situ thermal management are well established in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), comparable strategies remain far less explored in DED/LENS® because most systems lack tightly integrated, high-temperature platform control and studies have focused on parameter windows or post-deposition heat treatments. The limited DED literature that incorporates active in situ heating (e.g., heating plates or induction) [,] demonstrates clear benefits—lower cooling rates, reduced cracking, and altered phase evolution—but is focused on other tool steels or maraging grades rather than H13 and seldom targets controlled tempering during the build itself [].
